title: SCIS — Smart Cities Information System
text:
The problem
By the mid-2010s the Commission was funding a great many smart city projects — the FP7 portfolio, then the Horizon 2020 Smart Cities and Communities lighthouse projects — and had no systematic way of learning from them. Each project reported against its own indicators, in its own units, at its own boundary. Nothing was comparable, so nothing was transferable.
SCIS was the answer to that: a knowledge platform to gather, connect and disseminate data, experience and know-how from completed, ongoing and planned projects across energy, mobility and ICT, so that cities could see what had actually been tried elsewhere and what it had cost. AIT was a core partner.

title: SCIS — Smart Cities Information System
text:
The liveability question
The narrower problem I worked on was this. A smart city project can report an energy saving to two decimal places. It is much harder to say whether it made the place better to live in — and that, not the kilowatt-hours, is what a city council is actually buying.
The field was crowded with indicator frameworks, several of them EU-funded and running in parallel — CITYkeys and ESPRESSO alongside SCIS — and each carried implicit assumptions about what a good city is. Most existing frameworks were also either domain-specific (buildings, or energy, or transport) or aimed at ranking whole cities against each other, when what was needed was something that could evaluate the effect of a specific intervention on the people living around it.
The methodological difficulties are real ones:

Objective versus perceived. Measured noise levels and residents’ annoyance are only loosely correlated. Both are legitimate measures of the same thing; they do not agree.
Boundaries. A district-scale intervention has effects that leak — traffic displaced onto neighbouring streets, rents that rise, residents who move.
Aggregation and weighting. Collapsing a set of indicators into an index requires weights, and the weights encode a value judgement that the index then presents as arithmetic.
Distribution. A mean improvement is compatible with the worst-off group getting worse off.

title: SCIS — Smart Cities Information System
text:
My contribution
[This is the section only you can write — I couldn’t find a public deliverable that names your methodology work, so the notes below are prompts rather than findings.]
Worth covering:

What domains you settled on, and why those rather than the obvious energy-mobility-ICT split.
Which indicators you proposed, at what spatial scale, and what data sources were realistically available across the member states.
How you handled the objective/perceived split — survey instruments alongside measured data?
How the methodology related to CITYkeys and ESPRESSO: complementary, or a deliberate alternative?
Any city that actually applied it.

title: SCIS — Smart Cities Information System
text:
What I took from it
A durable scepticism about composite indices, and a preference for reporting the components alongside — and often instead of — the headline number. It also put liveability at the centre of how I think about transport work: a road safety or air quality intervention is ultimately justified by what it does to people’s daily experience of a street, and measuring that well is a genuinely unsolved problem rather than a box-ticking exercise.

title: CITYOPT — Optimising urban energy systems
text:
The problem
There are a great many ways to assemble a low-carbon district energy system — heat pumps, solar thermal, seasonal and short-term storage, waste heat recovery, electrical storage — and no obvious way to tell in advance which combination is best for a given site. The interactions are dynamic and non-linear: storage sizing depends on the production profile, which depends on the demand profile, which depends on the buildings, which depends on how the network is operated. Static spreadsheet feasibility studies flatten exactly the behaviour that determines whether the scheme works.
CITYOPT set out to build tools that let planners simulate, optimise and compare whole design alternatives rather than guess at them, covering the full lifecycle from strategic planning through detailed design to day-to-day operation.

title: CITYOPT — Optimising urban energy systems
text:
The approach
The project produced a planning tool structured around projects (a study area, with its input, output and external parameters) and scenarios (a particular set of parameter values describing one candidate design). Scenario outputs were generated by running an underlying dynamic simulation, with a genetic-algorithm optimiser searching the design space rather than the user enumerating options by hand.
The simulation engine for the Vienna case was Apros, a multifunctional dynamic process simulation tool with strong thermal-hydraulic component libraries — well suited to networks where flow, temperature and storage state all evolve together. The toolchain was released open source.

title: CITYOPT — Optimising urban energy systems
text:
My contribution
[Rewrite in your own words.]
I worked on the Vienna demonstration case: a concept and feasibility analysis for a micro district heating network fed by industrial waste heat rejected from a nearby industrial facility at several different temperature levels.
The system modelled comprised:

one standard office building and two energy-efficient office buildings as the heat sinks;
existing renewable supply — solar thermal collectors and heat pumps;
both short-term and long-term (seasonal) thermal storage, to balance the mismatch between when heat is rejected and when it is wanted.

The interesting part was the temperature cascade. Waste heat is not a single resource; it arrives at a range of grades, and the design question is which sink each grade should serve, and where a heat pump has to lift it. Getting that wrong means either dumping usable heat or running heat pumps against sources that could have supplied a load directly. Building this in Apros and letting the optimiser sweep network configurations, storage volumes and control setpoints made the trade-offs visible in a way a static calculation could not.
[Add specifics: annual recovered heat fraction, storage sizing conclusions, which configuration won, and what the buildings’ return temperatures did to the recovery potential.]

title: CITYOPT — Optimising urban energy systems
text:
What I took from it
That the temperature of energy matters as much as the quantity of it — a point that is obvious in thermodynamics and routinely lost in policy discussion, where waste heat gets counted as an undifferentiated megawatt-hour resource. It also gave me a lasting interest in storage as an arbitrage mechanism, thermal or electrical, which is more or less directly where my current work on battery arbitrage against dynamic tariffs came from.

title: ExpoSense
text:
The problem
Particulate matter is the largest environmental contributor to disease burden in the Netherlands: around 9,000 premature deaths a year are attributed to air pollution in the living environment alone, before you count occupational exposure.
The obstacle to doing much about it is resolution. Regulatory monitoring networks are sparse by design — a handful of stations per city, sited to represent broad conditions — while the exposure that matters to an individual happens at the scale of a street, a workshop, or the twenty minutes spent at a particular junction on the way to work. Modelling fills some of that gap but carries its own uncertainty. Meanwhile the arrival of cheap sensors inverted the problem: suddenly there was far more data than anyone had methods to interpret.

title: ExpoSense
text:
The approach
ExpoSense ran as an integrated programme across sensor development and data interpretation, with five interlocking strands:
1. Personal exposure profiles. Combining PM sensing with GPS tracking to build exposure profiles for individuals — where, when and from what source people are actually exposed, as a basis for feedback to vulnerable individuals and evidence for policymakers.
2. Population-level exposure maps. High concentrations are not the same thing as high exposure: a motorway at 3am and a school street at 8:30am are very different propositions for the same µg/m³. This strand combined dynamic PM concentration maps with information on how population is distributed in space and time, so that interventions could be targeted where the health consequences are greatest.
3. Crystalline silica sensor. Milling, sawing and drilling on construction sites generate crystalline silica dust with serious long-term health effects. A portable optical-spectroscopy device was developed to identify it in near real time, so exposure can be compared against occupational limits in an app while the work is happening rather than months later.
4. PM sensing with in-line chemical identification. Not all particulate matter is equally harmful — toxicity depends on chemical composition, which conventional PM sensors are blind to. This strand developed a device capable of chemically identifying particle types within complex mixtures.
5. Interpreting workplace exposure profiles. Synchronising exposure sensors with high-resolution contextual information about the conditions producing the exposure, so readings can be interpreted as they arrive. This ran on TNO’s EXCITE sensor data platform, which merges multiple high-resolution streams in real time and feeds a dashboard or app.

title: ExpoSense
text:
My contribution
[Adjust — I’ve assumed the population exposure mapping strand given your chemical transport modelling background, but correct this.]
My work sat on the population-level exposure mapping side: producing the dynamic concentration fields, and combining them with population dynamics to turn concentration into exposure.
Worth expanding on:

The modelling chain used to generate the concentration maps, and how sensor and reference-station data were brought in to constrain it.
How population dynamics were represented — mobility data, activity patterns, time-of-day weighting?
How the resulting exposure surfaces were validated, and what the honest uncertainty bounds were.
Anything that surprised you about where exposure concentrated once movement was accounted for.

title: ExpoSense
text:
What I took from it
The distinction between concentration and exposure is the one that has stayed with me, and it is routinely elided in air quality policy. A map of concentrations tells you about the air; a map of exposure tells you about people. They point at different places, and only the second one tells you where to intervene.
It is also the thread that connects directly to my current work on air quality effects of pop-up cycle lanes [link when live] — same question, different framing: what does a change to a street actually do to the air the people using it are breathing?

title: S4ECoB — Sounds for Energy Control of Buildings
text:
The problem
Buildings are among the largest energy consumers in Europe, and large public buildings — airports, shopping centres, stations — are among the least efficiently run of them. The reason is simple: their building management systems (BMS) are driven by schedules and setpoints, not by people. Heating, ventilation, air conditioning and lighting run to a timetable that assumes a worst-case crowd, whether the terminal holds four thousand passengers or four hundred.
Occupancy is the missing parameter. Measuring it directly at the scale of a whole terminal is awkward: turnstile counts miss most of the floor area, cameras are expensive and raise obvious privacy questions, and CO₂-based inference is slow and heavily damped by the ventilation system it is meant to be controlling.

title: S4ECoB — Sounds for Energy Control of Buildings
text:
The approach
S4ECoB took a less obvious route: listen.  The project developed a low-cost network of networked audio sensors, combined with sound and acoustic scene classification, to estimate occupancy level and its distribution across a building in near real time. That occupancy estimate was then exposed to the existing BMS as a new control input, so that HVACL operation could be matched to actual demand while keeping occupants comfortable.Occupied space sounds different from empty space, and the difference is measurable well before it shows up in a CO₂ trace.
Deliberately, the project worked with the building systems already installed rather than proposing a rip-and-replace: the value proposition was an integration layer and better control strategies, not new plant. The consortium committed to reporting quantified energy savings, CO₂ reduction, return on investment and payback time — an unusually hard-nosed set of deliverables for an FP7 ICT project.

title: S4ECoB — Sounds for Energy Control of Buildings
text:
My contribution
[Rewrite this section in your own words — the notes below are a scaffold.]
I built dynamic thermal models of the two demonstration buildings in TRNSYS:

Milano Linate Airport — a terminal with large glazed volumes, high infiltration through the landside doors, and a passenger load that swings hard with the flight schedule.
Maremagnum, Barcelona — a waterfront retail centre at Port Vell, with a very different occupancy signature: no timetable, strong weekday/weekend and seasonal structure, and internal gains dominated by lighting and retail units.

The models served two purposes. First, as a baseline: separating the building’s thermal response from the control strategy, so that measured savings during the demonstration could be attributed to the occupancy-driven control rather than to a mild winter. Second, as a testbed: running candidate control strategies against the simulated buildings, so that the sequences eventually deployed on the live BMS had already been sanity-checked against plausible occupancy profiles.
[Add specifics if you have them: which TRNSYS types, how the occupancy signal was coupled in, calibration against metered data, and the headline savings figure you arrived at.]

title: S4ECoB — Sounds for Energy Control of Buildings
text:
What I took from it
Two things stuck. The first is that in large public buildings the control strategy is usually a bigger lever than the fabric — you can chase U-values for years and get less than a well-tuned demand-driven ventilation schedule delivers in a season.
The second is the value of a calibrated baseline model. Without one, a demonstration project can only report a before-and-after difference, which is hopelessly confounded by weather and occupancy. This is the same argument I now make for meteorological normalisation of air quality data [link to the rmweather / pop-up cycle lane project when it’s up] — different domain, identical logic: you cannot claim an intervention effect until you have modelled away everything else that changed.
